13.2 Visualization and the Order Parameter
As our invocation of Speedy and Pokey in the last section suggests, it can
be helpful to visualize the oscillators as runners on a circular track-or, more
abstractly, as dots running around the unit circle.
Kuramoto Model 501
A great way to do this is to use colors to label the dots. Just as in the
electromagnetic spectrum where red corresponds to low frequency and violet
corresponds to high frequency, we can color the oscillator dots according to
their natural frequencies by following the usual rainbow ordering: red, orange,
yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. There are apps on the Internet that let you
simulate the Kuramoto model in this way, and they are fun to play with. A
terrific one is called "Ride my Kuramotocycle" by Dirk Brockmann (2018).
What you'll see is that the collective behavior of the swirling oscillator
dots depends on the strength of the couplingK. For one special case, we can
anticipate the results without even doing a simulation.
Example 13.2.1:
What happens if K =0 ?
Solution: If K =0 the oscillators are completely uncoupled. They don't
interact with each other at all; they just run around the circle at their own
natural frequencies according to˙Θi =Ω i. So the red dots-the slowest of the
slowpokes-fall behind the orange ones, which in turn lag behind the yellow
ones, and so on. Even if all the oscillators start in phase, the whole population
eventuallygetsscrambled,witharandommixofcoloreddotseverywhere.This
incoherentstate is totally desynchronized.■
Having dispensed with that easy case, we are still in the dark about what
to expect for K> 0. If we nudgeK up from zero, does the system start to
show signs of order? Or does it still lapse into incoherence, as it did forK =0 ?
Or maybe something weird and unexpected happens?
You should try this out on a computer for yourself, but since we don't
have access to an app here in the pages of this book, we will resort to a
statistical approach. It involves summarizing the overall degree of coherence
in the system by an average quantity called the complex order parameter.
Once that concept is in hand, we will return to the puzzle of what happens
as we increaseK.
Complex Order Parameter
Suppose we represent an oscillator with phaseΘj as a point in the(x, y) plane
at (cos Θj , sin Θj ). Notice that this point always lies on the unit circle, since
x2 + y2 = cos2 Θj +sin2 Θj =1 for any value ofΘj. Better yet, let's regard
that point as a complex number given by
x + iy = cos Θj + isin Θj = eiΘj
where the last equation follows from Euler's formula. Then the entire popu-
lation of oscillators corresponds toN points on the unit circle in the complex
plane.
Now take the average of the complex numberseiΘj . Let

In general, the radius (or magnitude)r of the complex order parameter
lies between zero and one. It measures the amount of phase coherence or order
in the population-that's why it's called theorder parameter. The angleΨ
is informative too; it provides a measure of the average phase.
To get some practice with these ideas, let's calculate the order parameter
for a few specific configurations of oscillators.
Example 13.2.2:

Or if you prefer to think geometrically, observe that since all the oscillators
are in phase, they all correspond to the same point on the unit circle. Thus
the population consists of that same point repeatedN times, and its centroid
is the point itself. Since that point lies on the unit circle, so does the centroid
and therefore r =1 . ■

Time Dependence of the Order Parameter
Now that we have defined the order parameterr, we can use it to assess how
the Kuramoto model behaves at different values ofK. The virtue of the order
parameter as a summary statistic is that it lets us see at a glance whether the
system is becoming more or less synchronized without having to keep track of
all N phases. Just the single numberr suffices.
Example 13.2.5:
Numerically integrate the Kuramoto model, using 1000 oscillators whose natu-
ral frequencies are randomly sampled from a Gaussian distribution with mean
µ =5and standard deviation σ =1 . Fix the coupling strength atK =1 .
Start all the oscillators in phase, and compute the time evolution of the order
parameter r(t). What happens in the long run?
Solution: Figure 13.2.3 shows thatr(t) plunges from r =1 and stays close
to r =0 thereafter, though with persistent fluctuations. Thus the system
loses its initial phase coherence. It falls apart, just like theK =0 system did!
Apparently K =1 is too small to enable the system to maintain itself in an
ordered state.
Figure 13.2.3
The fluctuations of r near zero are finite-size effects. They occur only
because N is finite; if N were infinite, r(t) would approach zero smoothly.
Intuitively, these fluctuations inr are what we'd get if we'd simply tossedN
points on a circle at random; it's as if the phases of the oscillators could be
anywhere. Using probability theory (Exercise 13.2.5) you can check that if
the oscillators really did have random phases, the fluctuations would have an
expected size r ≈ 1/
√
N, which decays to 0 asN →∞ . ■
Example 13.2.6:
Redo the simulation above, but now use a larger coupling strengthK =2 .5.
Startthesystemwithalowvalueof r byscatteringtheinitialphasesuniformly
at random over the interval0 < Θ < 15π/8. Compute the order parameter
r(t) until it settles down. What happens in this case?
Solution: Now the system becomes more and more ordered. The value of
r increases and then saturates at a level denoted byr∞ in Figure 13.2.4. The
small fluctuations ofr(t)about r∞ are finite-size effects that vanish asN →∞
(Exercise 13.2.4). ■

A Brave Guess
The simulations we've seen so far suggest that for the infinite-Nlimit of the
Kuramoto model, r(t) always approaches a constant in the long run.
Amazingly, Kuramoto (1975, 1984) guessed this resultwithout the benefit
of computer simulations! He simply assumedr was eventually constant and
carried out his analysis accordingly.
That was a pretty astonishing assumption-and a boldly optimistic one
at that! After all, we've seen that three-dimensional nonlinear dynamical sys-
tems, like the Lorenz and Rössler equations, typically don't settle down in the
long run. On the contrary, they display chaos that never stops. So why would
anyone think that a much higher-dimensional system would settle down to
something as simple as a constantr?
Whether by genius or good luck, Kuramoto turned out to be right. The
order parameter in his model alwaysdoes become constant as N →∞ and
t →∞ . This holds true for any value ofK ≥ 0 and any density G(Ω) with
the symmetric bell shape he assumed. Under those assumptions, the limiting
value of the order parameterr∞ depends onK in the manner shown in Figure
13.2.5.
Figure 13.2.5
Thereareseveralremarkablethingsaboutthispicture.Firstofall,itshows
that the system doesn't trivially get more ordered as we increase the coupling
strength K. Rather, the amount of order, as measured byr∞, remains at zero

--- Page 521 ---
506 Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos
until K reaches a critical valueKc. At that point, aphase transition occurs
and the system self-organizes into some kind of ordered state withr∞(K) > 0.
In the following sections we will see how Kuramoto pinpointed the nature of
that ordered state and thereby derived exact formulas forKc and r∞(K).

Kuramoto Model 507
Nevertheless, it tells us something important: it shows that the oscillators
interact only through the average quantities r and Ψ. In the language of
physics, the Kuramoto model is said to havemean-field coupling.
Our original point of view was that each oscillator is coupled to every
other oscillator. Our new point of view is that each one is coupled to the
mean field produced by all of them, the mean field being reflected in the
average quantitiesr and Ψ.
Intuitively, it's like being in a concert audience that's trying to clap in
unison. You could either listen to your individual neighbors and try to get in
sync with them, or you could listen to the collective rhythm in the whole room,
the sound of applause coming from everywhere in the concert hall. When you
try to get in sync with the overall sound, you are effectively interacting with
the mean field produced by everyone. You are not paying attention to any
individual member of the audience, only to the average of all of them.
View the Dynamics in a Rotating Frame
The next trick makes use of a symmetry in the Kuramoto model. If we imagine
viewing the dynamics in a reference frame rotating at a constant frequency,
it turns out that the governing equations stay the same. The oscillators still
obey the Kuramoto model-but with a shifted frequency.
In particular, suppose we go into a frame rotating at frequencyµ, the mean
frequency of the bell-shaped densityG(Ω). Let
θi =Θ i − µt
denote the phase of oscillatori in the rotating frame. Then
Θi = θi + µt
and therefore ˙Θi = ˙θi + µ. Substituting these expressions forΘi and ˙Θi into
˙Θi =Ω i + KN
N∑
j=1
sin (Θj − Θi)
(the governing equations for the Kuramoto model in the original frame), we
get
˙θi + µ =Ω i + KN
N∑
j=1
sin (θj + µt − [θi + µt]).
Now cancel the µt terms and subtractµ from both sides to obtain
˙θi =Ω i − µ + KN
N∑
j=1
sin (θj − θi). (2)
Equation (2) is the governing equation in the rotating frame-and, as

--- Page 523 ---
508 Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos
advertised, it's still the Kuramoto model! The only change is that in this
rotating frame, the natural frequency of oscillatori has effectively shifted to
ωi =Ω i − µ.
And sinceall the frequencies shift by this same amountµ, the mean frequency
now shifts toµ − µ =0 ; this will prove convenient in the calculations ahead.
In physical terms,ωi measures the sign and size of oscillatori's detuning
from the mean frequencyµ. It tells us whether oscillatori is faster or slower
than average, and by how much. Becauseωi is defined as Ωi − µ, oscillators
with a higher frequency than the mean haveωi > 0, whereas those with a
lower frequency haveωi < 0. Although we will often refer toωi as a frequency
or a shifted frequency when working in the rotating frame, the truth is that
it actually represents a detuning from the mean.
To see how the detunings are distributed across the population, denote
their associated probability density by
g(ω)= G(µ + ω).
Then because G was assumed to be symmetric about its mean, it satisfies
G(µ + ω)= G(µ − ω)
for all ω, which implies
g(ω)= g(−ω).
Thus g(ω) is an even function. This is one of the biggest advantages of working
in the rotating frame.

Locked Oscillators
Viewed in the rotating frame, the oscillators with|ωi| < Kr approach a stable
equilibrium point as t →∞ . To see this, consider the vector field for˙θi =
ωi − Kr sin θi when ωi > 0. (The oscillators withωi < 0 behave similarly.)
Figure 13.4.1
There are two fixed points on the unit circle, one of which is stable. In the
long run, all trajectories (except the one starting at the unstable fixed point)
satisfy θi(t) → θ∗i , where θ∗i is the solution of
Kr sin θ∗i = ωi (2)

These oscillators with|ωi|≤ Kr are said to bephase locked. Once they've
gotten stuck at their stable fixed points in the rotating frame, they remain
rigidlylockedataconstantphasedifferencerelativetooneanotherforalltime.

Viewed in the original frame, these locked oscillators run around the circle as a

fastest locked oscillators, those withωi = Kr, lead the way). And since they
all satisfy |ωi|≤ Kr, we see that they come from the middle of the frequency
distribution, shown here in gray in Figure 13.4.2. Their proximity to the mean
is what allows them to fall into rigid lockstep.

Kuramoto Model 511
Figure 13 .4.4
Keep in mind that all of this is happening in the rotating frame. Thus the
oscillators with |ωi| > Kr drift with respect to the locked group. The fast
ones run ahead of the group and the slow ones fall behind it. They cannot
synchronize with the group because their frequencies are too far from the
mean.
The distinction between locked and drifting oscillators is especially strik-
ing in computer simulations. If you watch the model evolve by visualizing it as
a swarm of colored dots running around the unit circle, then the locked group
appears as a rainbow-colored block of oscillators drawn from the middle of
the spectrum (orange, yellow, green, blue). The fastest (blue) oscillators posi-
tion themselves at the front of the pack, and the slowest (orange) oscillators
bring up the rear. Meanwhile, the oscillators at the extremes of the frequency
distribution-the very slow red ones in the left tail of the distribution, and
the very fast violet ones in the right tail-drift away from the synchronized
pack. They either fall behind the pack and keep getting lapped by it if they're
super-slow, or they race ahead of it and keep lapping it if they're super-fast.
The Puzzle Posed by the Drifting Oscillators
Our analysis so far has shown that if steady solutions exist, they must consist
of locked oscillators, drifting oscillators, or both types of oscillators (in which
case we say the system ispartially locked or partially synchronized).
Buthowcoulddriftingoscillatorsbecompatiblewiththeassumedconstant
values of r and ψ? With all those wild oscillators buzzing around the circle,
how can the system keep its centroid constant? If it doesn't, our analysis
becomes self-contradictory and collapses.
Kuramoto proposed a brilliant solution to this puzzle. He suggested that
if the drifters arrange themselves according to astationary distribution, they

--- Page 527 ---
512 Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos
would contribute a constant amount tor and ψ and everything could be made
consistent.
Stationary Distribution of the Drifting Oscillators
To derive a formula for the stationary distribution, consider all the drifting
oscillators that have some particular natural frequencyω, and suppose there
areinfinitelymanyofthem.Picturethemasacoloredfluidswirlingaroundthe
circle. The individual molecules (oscillators) in this fluid move nonuniformly
according to a velocity field given by
v(θ, ω)= ˙θ
= ω − Kr sin θ.
In steady state, the oscillator fluid will be densely distributed where the ve-
locity field is slow and thinly distributed where it's fast (intuitively, it's like
how traffic gets most congested on the part of the highway where the cars
are moving slowest). Even though individual oscillators continue to move, the
distribution as a whole can remain stationary, as one oscillator moves out of
the way for another to replace it.
These considerations led Kuramoto to guess that the drifters would dis-
tribute themselves on the circle with a density inversely proportional to the
local speed atθ:
ρ(θ, ω)= C|ω − Kr sin θ| . (3)
For ω > Kr the density looks like that shown in Figure 13.4.5.
Figure 13.4.5
The velocityv(θ, ω)= ω − Kr sin θ is closest to zero atθ = π/2, which is why
the density has its peak there.

13.5 Self-Consistency
The next task is to carry out a self-consistency calculation. The stationary
states of the locked and drifting oscillators found above must be consistent
with the constant values ofr and ψ we originally assumed.
Specifically, the complex order parameter reiψ must be self-consistent.
Thus
reiψ = ⟨eiθ ⟩ (1)
where the angle brackets denote an average over the population. Imposing the
assumption thatψ ≡ 0in the rotating frame, thisself-consistency equation
becomes
r = ⟨eiθ ⟩.
There are two contributions to the average on the right-hand side, one from
the locked oscillators and another from the drifting oscillators. Thus
r = ⟨eiθ ⟩lock + ⟨eiθ ⟩drift. (2)
Let's calculate each of these contributions in turn.

The reasoning behind this formula is similar to that for the locked oscillators,
but slightly more involved. To averageeiθ over the drifting oscillators, we have
to account first for what fraction of them have a particular phaseθ, given that
they also have a particular frequencyω; this fraction is proportional to the
density ρ(θ, ω). Then we have to weight that contribution according tog(ω),
the density of oscillators that happen to have that frequency. And finally we
have to integrate over all possible frequencies and phases.

So in steady state, the drifters contribute nothing to the order parameter.
Ironically, after worrying that they could wreck our whole analysis, we find
that they cancel each other out. They're as harmless as could be.

Example 13.5.2:
Interpret the formula forKc. What is it saying, and why does it make sense
intuitively?
Solution: The key is to understand what1/g(0) means. First observe that
g(0) is the height of the graph ofg(ω), since g is assumed to be even and
unimodal (Figure 13.5.4). Also, the total area under the graph equals 1, since
g isaprobabilitydensity.Therefore,arectanglewiththesameheightandtotal
area asg(ω) would have a width of1/g(0). In that sense,1/g(0) measures the
width of g. It tells us how diverse the oscillators are by quantifying their spread
of natural frequencies about the mean.
Figure 13.5.4
This notion of width is proportional to the standard deviation ofg, the
usual measure of width for densities that have a finite standard deviation.
For heavy-tailed distributions with an infinite standard deviation,1/g(0) still
usefully measures the width even when the standard deviation becomes mean-
ingless.
Withthisinterpretationinhand,wenowseethattheresult Kc = 2/[πg(0)]
says that the critical coupling is proportional to the width of the frequency
distribution. That makes sense: if the oscillators are more diverse, they need
a larger K to get them to start synchronizing.■

Locking Threshold
So far we have assumed the densityg(ω) has infinite tails. Because there are
oscillators with arbitrarily largeω, any steady state of the infinite-Nmodel is
guaranteed to include a sub-population of drifters-oscillators from the tails
whose frequencies satisfy|ω| > Kr ∞ and which therefore cannot synchronize
with the locked group. Hence, completely-locked steady states are impossible
if g has infinite tails.
But now suppose g(ω) doesn't have infinite tails. Instead, imagine that
g(ω) is supported on a finite interval, meaning that there's some maximum
frequency ωmax such that g(ω)=0 for all |ω| >ω max. Then complete locking
becomes possible! It occurs onceK exceeds alocking threshold K = KL. At
this bifurcation point,all the oscillators become phase locked and no drifters
remain. Exercises 13.5.7 and 13.5.8 invite you to calculate the locking thresh-
old for two convenient special cases.
One last thing: If you're feeling confused about the difference betweenKc
and KL, here's a good way to think about it. Phase locking begins in the
population at K = Kc and becomes complete atK = KL.
13.6 Remaining Questions
Our analysis leaves many questions unanswered. For instance, it shows only
that steady statesexist for the infinite-N limit of the Kuramoto model, but it
says nothing about whether they arestable. Kuramoto (1984) openly worried
about this issue. Settling it took a few more decades of research (Strogatz
2000, Mirollo and Strogatz 2007, Ott and Antonsen 2008, Ott and Antonsen
2009, Chiba 2015, Engelbrecht and Mirollo 2020).
Another subtlety concerns what happens ifN is large but finite, rather
than infinite. Can one prove that the behavior of the finite-N model converges
in some sense to that predicted by the infinite-Nanalysis? And what ifN is

--- Page 535 ---
520 Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos
small? Some progress has been made on these questions, but it's fair to say a
lot remains to be discovered.
Indeed, there are countless directions left to explore. We could consider
other networks than the complete graph. We could change the nature of the
oscillators, allowing them to have variable amplitude as well as phase. We
could investigate quantum or stochastic generalizations of the model.
And, of course, we could ask whether the model tells us anything about the
real world. Kuramoto devised his equations on purely aesthetic grounds. He
was looking for an exactly solvable many-oscillator system that could display
a synchronization transition. But do anyreal physical, chemical, or biological
systems behave like the Kuramoto model? Actually, yes. It turns out that large
systems of Josephson junctions, metronomes, electrochemical oscillators, and
generators in the power grid are pretty well described by the model, at least in
certain limits (Wiesenfeld et al. 1998, Pantaleone 2002, Kiss et al. 2002, Fila-
trella et al. 2008). And with regard to the original motivating examples from
biology-brain waves, fireflies flashing in unison, yeast cells displaying oscil-
latory glycolysis, human concert audiences clapping in sync-the Kuramoto
model has prompted new experiments and sharpened old questions (Néda et
al. 2000, Danø et al. 2009, Weber et al. 2020, Sarfati et al. 2021). It has
even found medical application, for example to the modeling of deep brain
stimulation used to treat Parkinson's disease (Tass 1999, Tass 2003).
Parting Thoughts
We have come to the end of our journey together, but there is so much more
to learn! I wish you all the best on your next adventures and thank you for
joining me on this one. I hope you've enjoyed it as much as I have.

13.1.7 (Deriving Kuramoto from van der Pol) The Kuramoto model some-

¨xi + ϵ(xi2 − 1) ˙xi + (1 + ϵωi)xi = ϵ κN

˙xj
for i =1 , ...,N . At zeroth order (ϵ=0 ) this is a collection of un-

have a system of weakly nonlinear oscillators of the type we studied
in Section 7.6.
The system includes three small perturbations whose effects accumu-

being identical, through the ϵωi term. Third, the system is weakly
coupled in an all-to-all fashion through theϵκ term on the right-hand
side.

coupled in an all-to-all fashion through theϵκ term on the right-hand
side.

13.4.3 (A chain of oscillators) Applied mathematicians have used chains of
phase oscillators to model a wide variety of biological phenomena,
from neuromuscular waves in the mammalian intestine (Ermentrout
and Kopell 1984, Winfree 1980) to stomatal oscillations in the leaves
of green plants (Rand et al. 1982). One of the most celebrated ap-
plications involves an organism known as a lamprey, a scary-looking,
eel-like creature much beloved of neuroscientists but hardly anyone
else. In conjunction with sensory signals coming from its muscles, a
lamprey's undulatory swimming rhythm is coordinated by a "central
pattern generator," a neural network that produces waves of electri-
cal activity along its body. Treating this central pattern generator
as a chain of oscillators, Rand et al. (1988) discussed the following
simplified model:
˙θ1 = ω1 + asin(θ2 − θ1),
˙θi = ωi + asin(θi−1 − θi)+a sin(θi+1 − θi),i =2 ,...,N − 1
˙θN = ωN + asin(θN −1 − θN )

13.4.4 (Coupled spins with random pinning) The dynamical system
˙θi = sin(αi − θi)+ KN
N∑
j=1
sin(θj − θi),i = 1,...,N
has been used to model the behavior of a large collection of globally
coupled magnetic spins subject to local pinning fields. The variables
θ1,...,θ N represent the directions of the spin vectors, abstracted as
points on the unit circle. What makes the model interesting is that
it pits two conflicting forces against one another: a pinning force of
unit strength tries to make eachθi point in its own preferred direction
αi while a coupling force of strengthK ≥ 0 tries to make all theθi
the same. The trouble comes if the preferred anglesα1,...,α N vary a
lot across the population; then it's impossible to please everyone. In
human terms, it's like the quandary faced by a group of friends who
all want to eat together but they have trouble deciding on a restaurant
because everybody likes a different kind of cuisine.

waveform, but they are separated in time by a fixed fraction of a cycle:

for k =1 , ..., N. Here, Φ is the common waveform andT is the oscil-
lation period in the sense thatΦ(t + T ) = Φ( t)+2 π for all t.

13.6.2 (Global synchronization on random graphs) As of this writing, very
little is known about the dynamics of the Kuramoto model on an
arbitrary network, even for the homogeneous model (1) where the
oscillators are identical.
The question about model (1) that has received the most attention
concerns the global stability of the "in-phase" or "synchronized" state
(meaning any state withθi = θj for all i, j). What happens on net-
works of different sizes and wiring diagrams? Are some networks bet-
ter at synchronizing than others?
In 2019, Ling et al. (2019) explored what they called the "average-case
scenario" for a network of sizeN. To do so, they considered Erdős-
Rényi random graphs, where any pair of nodes have a probabilityp
of being connected. In other words,aij =1 with probability p, and
aij =0 with probability1 − p. All theaij are picked independently at
random, subject to the symmetry constraintaij = aji. Here0 ≤ p ≤ 1
is an adjustable parameter that controls how densely interconnected
the graph is. This exercise asks you to investigate system (1)'s long-
term behavior asp and N vary, using numerical simulation.
a) Try small values ofN, say between 5 and 100, and varyp in small
steps between 0 and 1. Run 50 simulations at each(N, p) pair, and
record how many of them end up in an in-phase state.
b) Compare your results to those in Ling et al. (2019, Fig. 5).
c) Learn about phase transitions in random graphs. What did Erdős
and Rényi discover? How do their results relate to those found in
parts (a) and (b)?
As a grand finale, we conclude with three exercises leading up to perhaps the
biggest breakthrough in our understanding of the Kuramoto model in the past
50 years. It goes by the name of theOtt-Antonsen ansatz . It shows that
the Kuramoto model, and many of its closely related cousins, can be reduced
exactly to low-dimensional dynamical systems, even though their governing
equations are infinite-dimensional! See the original paper by Ott and Antonsen
(2008), as well as the reviews by Pikovsky and Rosenblum (2015) and Bick et
al. (2020) for more information about this work and its impact.
